summary: Describes the Camellia block cipher in Counter mode and Counter with CBC-MAC mode, and provides test vectors. The goal is to make Camellia-CTR and Camellia-CCM easily available to the Internet community.

eli5.summary: Camellia is a way of scrambling data. This note explains two ways of using it on long messages, with sample answers so builders can check their work.

subtitle: Test vectors for two encryption modes of the Camellia block cipher

tldr.problem: The Camellia block cipher has been standardized internationally, but implementations need clear test vectors to verify that their Camellia-CTR and Camellia-CCM implementations are correct and interoperable.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how Camellia operates in Counter mode (for stream-like encryption) and Counter with CBC-MAC mode (for authenticated encryption), and provides 33 test vectors covering different key sizes and message lengths to validate implementations.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can verify their cryptographic libraries produce correct results, ensuring secure and interoperable encrypted communications using Camellia in modern cipher modes.

today: RFC 5528 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It serves as a reference for implementers of Camellia-CTR and Camellia-CCM, ensuring interoperable and correct cryptographic implementations.

sections.title: Camellia: A Standardized Block Cipher
sections.content:
Camellia is a symmetric block cipher developed jointly by NTT and Mitsubishi Electric in 2000. It operates on 128-bit blocks and supports key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits—the same interface as AES (Advanced Encryption Standard).

Camellia has been adopted as an international standard by ISO/IEC and is recommended by the EU's NESSIE project and Japan's CRYPTREC program. It is widely implemented in open source projects including OpenSSL, FreeBSD, and Linux. The RFC is published to make Camellia-CTR and Camellia-CCM easily accessible to the Internet community by specifying these modes and providing test vectors for implementation verification.
sections.eli5: Camellia is a way of scrambling data that is recognized by countries around the world. This document explains two popular ways to use it for encrypting messages.

sections.title: How Camellia Works
sections.content:
Camellia is a Feistel network block cipher, meaning it processes data in discrete 128-bit blocks by repeatedly applying rounds of substitution and permutation. The cipher supports three key sizes: 128 bits (required for all implementations), and 192 and 256 bits (optional). There are no known weak keys for Camellia.

Because Camellia uses a fixed 128-bit block size, any data to be encrypted must be padded to a multiple of 16 octets (128 bits). The cipher specification is published in RFC 3713, and this RFC builds on that foundation by describing how to use Camellia with stream and authenticated-encryption modes.
sections.eli5: Camellia takes a secret key and scrambles 16-byte chunks of data in a complicated way. All three key sizes (16, 24, or 32 bytes) work; bigger keys are slightly harder to break.

sections.title: Counter Mode: Stream-Like Encryption
sections.content:
Counter (CTR) mode turns a block cipher into a stream cipher. Instead of encrypting each block of plaintext directly, CTR mode encrypts counter blocks (containing a nonce and an incrementing counter) to produce a keystream, then XORs the plaintext with this keystream.

The advantage is that CTR mode does not require padding—you can encrypt any number of bytes. The mode also allows parallel encryption of multiple blocks, since each counter block is independent. This RFC specifies how Camellia-CTR works, with the nonce forming part of the counter block and the counter field incrementing for each successive block.

The RFC provides nine test vectors for Camellia-CTR, covering encryptions with 128-bit, 192-bit, and 256-bit keys, encrypting 16 to 36 octets of plaintext. Each vector shows the plaintext, key, IV, counter blocks, keystream output, and resulting ciphertext to allow implementers to verify their code.
sections.eli5: CTR mode pretends Camellia is a way to generate random-looking numbers. You feed it a counter that increments, and it gives you random-looking bytes. You mix those with your message to hide it. This way, any length message works, not just multiples of 16.

sections.title: Counter with CBC-MAC Mode: Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) mode combines encryption with authentication. It encrypts the plaintext using CTR mode and simultaneously computes a Message Authentication Code (MAC) using cipher block chaining to ensure the message has not been tampered with.

CCM is useful for security protocols that need both confidentiality (secrecy) and authenticity (proof that the sender created the message). The mode can optionally include cleartext header data that is authenticated but not encrypted. The authentication tag is typically 8 or 10 octets long.

This RFC provides 24 test vectors for Camellia-CCM, each showing the cleartext header, plaintext, nonce, resulting ciphertext, and authentication tag. The vectors use the standard 13-octet nonce length and various message lengths to validate CCM implementations.
sections.eli5: CCM mode is CTR mode plus a signature. It scrambles your message like CTR does, but also computes a checksum that proves nobody changed the message on the way.

sections.title: Test Vectors and Verification
sections.content:
The RFC contains 33 test vectors total: 9 for Camellia-CTR and 24 for Camellia-CCM. Each vector specifies the key, initialization values (IV), plaintext, and the correct ciphertext and authentication output. Implementers run their code with these inputs and verify that the output matches the expected result.

For Camellia-CTR, vectors cover all three key sizes (128, 192, 256 bits) with plaintext lengths of 16, 32, and 36 octets. For Camellia-CCM, vectors use a 128-bit key and test both 8-octet and 10-octet authentication tags, with varying header and message lengths.

These test vectors come from the official Camellia web site and allow developers to gain confidence that their implementation is correct before deploying it in production systems.
sections.eli5: The document gives you a bunch of real examples: "if you use this key, nonce, and message, you should get this encrypted output." You check your code against all the examples.
